Appreciate the transparency, Ben. What surprised me is how much personal conviction sits alongside the evidence in your portfolio.

A roughly 33% allocation to Canada versus its ~3% global market weight is a substantial home bias, especially with your home and career already tied to Canada. Tax advantages and behavioural considerations may justify some overweight, but do they justify this much?

The factor tilts have an academic foundation, but choosing the factors, their weights and Dimensional’s implementation still requires judgment. Better explanatory power in an asset-pricing model doesn’t automatically establish superior future returns after costs. Similarly, the lifecycle paper’s one-third domestic allocation is a model-dependent result, not a universal prescription.

The employer-related equity seems the clearest concentration risk. Buying PWL shares at an attractive valuation while helping build the business makes sense. Continuing to hold OneDigital is a separate investment decision. Past success and personal attachment don’t establish its attractiveness today, although having enough diversified wealth elsewhere may make that risk entirely affordable.

The house and cash actually seem easier to reconcile: stability, enjoyment and liquidity have value beyond investment returns. Also, “all equity” describes your long-term investment allocation, not your entire balance sheet.

My takeaway: this is a personally tailored portfolio with deliberate trade-offs, rather than an obvious endpoint of evidence-based investing. Where do you draw the line between a justified deviation from the market portfolio and a preference we’re good at rationalizing?

Canada is 3% of the world market. a 30% home country bias is massive. You are placing 10 times the amount of capital into Canada compared to market weights. Per Bill Sharpe, any allocation away from cap weights is an active bet. If you think that a home country bias is good because of home country vs foreign stock volatilities/currency risk, I hate to say it - but you have hindsight bias. For example - for a US investor in the past 50 years, a 55-60% US, rest international allocation has been the lowest volatility portfolio. However, that number can and will change. It's all based on correlations of home country vs international, as well as the volatilities of each. 
Vanguard came out and said US investors' optimal allocation is around 60 to 80% US, rest in international. They also said Canadians should allocate around 30% of assets to Canada. Both of those studies were basically just looking at historical data and asking "what portfolio would have had the lowest volatility?" The answer is from foreign and home country stock market concentration, size, currency volatility, and correlations. That's it. If you think you know what those data points will be for your home country and foreign, you can calculate the optimal, lowest variance portfolio. However, this isn't possible. Forecasting correlations, vols, etc is as easy as picking the right stocks - and that's also impossible. If Canadians live through an era of high stock market concentration/volatility, low CAD volatility, and different correlations than in the past, then the "optimal" low variance allocation to home country stocks for a Canadian investor will shrink dramatically! Same in reverse. If you can't predict those, then the best thing is just be market cap weighted. I think home country bias is great if it helps you hold tight and stick with your strategy, but that's it. It's not alpha for investors to concentrate exposure in anything - tech sector, growth, value, home country, US, whatever.
